## What [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) decides for you

Building search on the lower-level
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
means choosing an encoder, a vector type, a chunk size, how to query,
and whether to build a document tree, before the first result.
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) makes
all of these choices from the measurements in `evals/` and leaves you
one: whether to rerank.

The scores below are weighted section MRR over three corpora with 120
queries each. MRR (mean reciprocal rank) is 1 when the right section
comes first, 1/2 when it comes second, and so on, averaged over the
queries.

`Index.db` is the
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
you would have built by hand, and every function from the lower level
works on it.

## [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)

Three lines give you a searchable collection:

``` python
ix = Index('kb.db')
ix.add('docs/')
ix.search('how does batching work')
```

An [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)
holds an encoder, a store of chunks and a document tree. Each method is
a short call into `litesearch.core` or `litesearch.tree` with the
measured defaults already filled in, so anything
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) does
you can also do by hand with those modules.

`encoder` can be any object with an `encode` method that takes a list of
strings, or a
[`FastEncode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#fastencode).
The store records the encoder’s name when it has one (see
[`encoder_id`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#encoder_id)),
and reopening the file with a differently named encoder raises
[`StoreMismatch`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#storemismatch),
because vectors from two models cannot be compared.

### Index

``` python
def Index(
    path:str=':memory:', # sqlite file; omit for in-memory
    encoder:NoneType=None, # an object with `.encode`, or a `FastEncode` (default: static potion-multilingual-128M)
    name:str='store', # chunk table, if you want several corpora in one file
    ann:bool=True, # maintain an HNSW index for the vector leg
    db:NoneType=None, # an open Database to share, for several corpora in one file
):
```

*A searchable collection: add files, code or text, then query it with a
string.*

### Adding documents

`add` takes what you have: a directory, a file path, a string, a list of
strings, or a `{title: text}` dict. Documents go through
`litesearch.tree`, which keeps each document’s heading structure, so
every chunk knows the section it came from. For a directory, `types`
lists the file extensions to pick up. `add` returns the change in the
store’s chunk count: 0 when every text was already stored, and negative
when an edit shortened a document. One text is stored once. A file’s
source is its resolved path, a copy or a string with stored text only
records its source, and a file edited since it was added replaces its
old chunks. Each hit carries its document’s `source`, and `docs` lists
every source a document is stored for. `remove(src)` forgets a file, URL
or title; its text stays while another source shares it. The tree page
has the full contract.

Source code goes through `add_code` instead. It reads a directory or an
installed package. Python files are cut at top-level functions and
classes using Python’s own parser, other source files become one chunk
per function signature (through codesigs), and any notebooks, Markdown,
text or PDF files it finds are chunked as text. Each file becomes one
document of kind `code` with a single node, under the same rules as
`add`: a file re-added unchanged or copied writes nothing, and an edited
file replaces its chunks. Each chunk’s file path and definition name are
kept in its `metadata`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/blob/main/litesearch/api.py#L68"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

``` python
def add(
    src, # directory, file path, string, list of strings, or {title: text}
    types:str='.pdf,.md,.markdown,.txt,.rst,.ipynb,.xml,.tei,.htm,.html,.conllu', # extensions to pick up when `src` is a directory
    **kw
)->int: # forwarded to add_dir / add_file / add_doc
```

*Add documents or text to the index and return the change in its chunk
count, negative when an edit shortened a document.*

def add_code(

    force:bool=False, # rewrite files whose code is already stored
    **kw

*Add the source code in a directory or installed package, one document

written.*

### Searching

`search` runs the hybrid search: an FTS5 keyword query and a vector
search, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Pass a string and get chunks
back, best first. Neighbouring hits from the same section are merged
into one, and each hit has a `breadcrumb`, the path of headings above
it, so you can cite where it came from. `where` takes a SQL condition on
the store’s columns, such as `doc_id='...'`, to search part of the
collection.

`rerank=True` is the one setting the evaluation leaves to you. It takes
`RERANK_FANOUT` (30) candidates and reorders them with a flashrank
cross-encoder, a model that reads the query and each candidate together.
That gained 0.026 to 0.077 weighted MRR, better in all twelve paired
cells measured, at roughly 10 times the query time and a small model
download the first time. The number of candidates matters: reranking ten
candidates can only reorder those ten, and the measured gain comes from
reranking thirty.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/blob/main/litesearch/api.py#L120"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### Index.search

``` python
def search(
    q:str, # query string
    limit:int=10, # hits to return
    rerank:bool=False, # reorder the top 30 candidates with a flashrank cross-encoder
    where:str=None, # SQL over the chunk store, to search part of it
    **kw
)->list: # forwarded to Database.doc_search
```

*Hybrid keyword and vector search, returning chunks with neighbouring
hits merged and a breadcrumb on each.*

### Reading

The document tree is built at ingest whether you use it or not, because
it costs nothing in ranking. It is what these four methods need, and
they are the reason to keep it.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>method</th>
<th>what it answers</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>toc()</code></td>
<td>what is in the collection, as a nested table of contents. It reads
no embeddings</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>sections(q)</code></td>
<td>which sections are about the query, rather than which 512-byte
chunks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>read(node_id)</code></td>
<td>the whole text of one section, put back together from its
chunks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>context(q)</code></td>
<td>the sections that best answer the query, with their text and
position in the tree, plus related sections, ready to give a language
model</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

On the Sanskrit corpus, `context` nearly doubles verse-level recall over
plain chunk search, from 0.190 to 0.340. That is the largest single
effect measured anywhere in `evals/`, larger than any change of encoder.
Putting sections back together helps even though ranking by section does
not.

## Worked example

Five short documents, added as text so the cell runs anywhere.

``` python
ix = Index()
ix.add({'Batching': 'Requests are batched by the scheduler before they reach the model. '
                    'Batch size trades latency for throughput.',
        'Caching':  'A prompt cache stores the prefix of a request so that repeated prefixes '
                    'skip recomputation entirely.',
        'Sharding': 'Large models are sharded across devices; each shard holds a slice of every '
                    'weight matrix.',
        'Metrics':  'Throughput is tokens per second. Latency is time to first token.',
        'Retries':  'Failed requests are retried with exponential backoff and a jitter term.'})
ix
```

### Several collections in one file

`db=` gives an
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) a
database that is already open, so two
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)
objects can be two stores in one file. They must share the connection,
not only the path: `database(':memory:')` called twice gives two
separate databases, and two connections to one file on disk compete for
one write lock.

Each store keeps its own chunks, its own tree and its own HNSW index, so
a query on one never sees the other. They cannot share a vector space,
though. An HNSW index holds one encoder’s vectors, and distances between
two encoders’ vectors mean nothing. If the two collections use different
encoders, search each one separately and merge the results by rank, for
example with
[`rrf_all`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#rrf_all).

``` python
dbf = database()                                    # one file, opened once
main, papers = Index(db=dbf), Index(db=dbf, name='papers')
main.add({'Batching': 'Throughput rises with batch size until the device runs out of memory.'})
papers.add({'Scaling': 'Loss follows a power law in parameters, data and compute.'})
([d['title'] for d in main.docs], [d['title'] for d in papers.docs])
```

    (['Batching'], ['Scaling'])

## Going below [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)

[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) is one
of two routes, and the other stays available. Go below it when you need
something it decides for you:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>you want</th>
<th>use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>SQL over your own columns, joins, filters</td>
<td><code>ix.db</code>, a plain <a
href="https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database"><code>database()</code></a></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>a different encoder, or float32 vectors</td>
<td><a
href="https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database"><code>database()</code></a>
and <code>get_store()</code> directly</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>several stores, or a custom FTS5 tokenizer</td>
<td><code>db.get_store(name=..., tokenize=...)</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>entity-graph retrieval for questions that share no words with the
answer</td>
<td><code>db.graph_search</code>, added by <a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/vruksha">vruksha</a> when you
import it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>matching Sanskrit across scripts</td>
<td><code>litesearch.sanskrit</code>, see <a
href="09_sanskrit.ipynb">sanskrit</a></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sanskrit metre, verse trees, lemmas</td>
<td><a href="https://github.com/vedicreader/ganapati">ganapati</a></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) does
not offer the graph search at all, because it measured negative. On
ordinary known-item queries it lowers weighted MRR by 0.070 to 0.160. On
a set of 120 questions per corpus built to favour it, where the answer
shares no word with the question, it raised target MRR by only 0.004 and
0.014 on the two corpora tried, while the score for the easy part of
each question, the passage keyword search finds directly, fell by about
21% and taking 3 to 5 times as long. `evals/RESULTS.md` has the method.
Use `db.graph_search` only when you know your questions look like that.

## vishalakshi

[vishalakshi](https://github.com/vedicreader/vishalakshi) is a document
vault built on litesearch. Its `Vault` class is a subclass of
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index), and
its search, sections, context and read call
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)’s
methods. It is the largest user of this API, so a change to
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) should
be checked against it.
